{{short description|Result on the class group of certain number fields, strengthening Ernst Kummer's theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Herbrand–Ribet theorem''' is a result on the [[class group]] of certain [[number field]]s. It is a strengthening of [[Ernst Kummer]]'s theorem to the effect that the [[prime number|prime]] ''p'' divides the [[ideal class group|class number]] of the [[cyclotomic field]] of ''p''-th [[roots of unity]] [[if and only if]] ''p'' divides the numerator of the ''n''-th [[Bernoulli number]] ''B''<sub>''n''</sub> 
for some ''n'', 0 < ''n'' < ''p'' − 1. The Herbrand–Ribet theorem specifies what, in particular, it means when ''p'' divides such an ''B<sub>n</sub>''.

== Statement ==
The [[Galois group]] &Delta; of the [[cyclotomic field]] of ''p''th roots of unity for an [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] prime ''p'', '''Q'''(&zeta;) with &zeta;<sup>''p''</sup> = 1, consists of the ''p'' − 1 group elements &sigma;<sub>''a''</sub>, where <math>\sigma_a(\zeta) = \zeta^a</math>. As a consequence of [[Fermat's little theorem]], in the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of [[p-adic integer|''p''-adic integers]] <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math> we have ''p'' &minus; 1 roots of unity, each of which is congruent mod ''p'' to some number in the range 1 to ''p'' &minus; 1; we can therefore define a [[Dirichlet character]] &omega; (the Teichmüller character) with values in <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math> by requiring that for ''n'' relatively prime to ''p'', &omega;(''n'') be congruent to ''n'' modulo ''p''. The ''p'' part of the class group is a <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>-module (since it is ''p''-primary), hence a module over the [[group ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}_p[\Delta]</math>. We now define [[idempotent element]]s of the group ring for each ''n'' from 1 to ''p'' − 1, as

:<math>\epsilon_n = \frac{1}{p-1}\sum_{a=1}^{p-1} \omega(a)^n \sigma_a^{-1}.</math>

It is easy to see that <math>\sum\epsilon_n = 1 </math> and <math> \epsilon_i\epsilon_j = \delta_{ij}\epsilon_i </math> where <math> \delta_{ij} </math> is the [[Kronecker delta]]. This allows us to break up the ''p'' part of the ideal class group ''G'' of '''Q'''(&zeta;) by means of the idempotents; if ''G'' is the ''p''-primary part of the ideal class group, then, letting ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> = &epsilon;<sub>''n''</sub>(''G''), we have <math> G = \oplus G_n </math>.

The Herbrand–Ribet theorem states that for odd ''n'', ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> is nontrivial if and only if ''p'' divides the Bernoulli number ''B''<sub>''p''&minus;''n''</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ribet |first=Ken |title=A modular construction of unramified p-extensions of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>(&mu;<sub>p</sub>) |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae|Inv. Math.]] |volume=34 |issue=3 |year=1976 |pages=151–162 |doi=10.1007/bf01403065|s2cid=120199454 }}</ref> 

The theorem makes no assertion about even values of ''n'', but there is no known ''p'' for which ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> is nontrivial for any even ''n'': triviality for all ''p'' would be a consequence of [[Vandiver's conjecture]].<ref>{{cite book | first1=John | last1=Coates | authorlink1=John Coates (mathematician) | first2=R. | last2=Sujatha | authorlink2=Sujatha Ramdorai | title=Cyclotomic Fields and Zeta Values | series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=2006 | isbn=3-540-33068-2 | zbl=1100.11002 | pages=3–4 }}</ref>

== Proofs ==
The part saying ''p'' divides ''B''<sub>''p''&minus;''n''</sub> if ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> is not trivial is due to [[Jacques Herbrand]].<ref>{{cite journal | zbl=0006.00802 | last=Herbrand | first=J. | title=Sur les classes des corps circulaires | language=French | journal=J. Math. Pures Appl. |series=Série IX | volume=11 | pages=417–441 | year=1932 | issn=0021-7824 }}</ref> The converse, that if ''p'' divides ''B''<sub>''p''&minus;''n''</sub> then ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> is not trivial is due to [[Kenneth Ribet]], and is considerably more difficult. By [[class field theory]], this can only be true if there is an unramified extension of the field of ''p''th roots of unity by a [[cyclic extension]] of degree ''p'' which behaves in the specified way under the action of &Sigma;; Ribet proves this by actually constructing such an extension using methods in the theory of [[modular form]]s. A more elementary proof of Ribet's converse to Herbrand's theorem, a consequence of the theory of [[Euler system]]s, can be found in Washington's book on cyclotomic fields.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Washington |first=Lawrence C. |title=Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields |edition=Second |location=New York |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1997 |isbn=0-387-94762-0 }}</ref>

== Generalizations ==
Ribet's methods were developed further by [[Barry Mazur]] and [[Andrew Wiles]] in order to prove the [[main conjecture of Iwasawa theory]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mazur |first1=Barry |name-list-style=amp |last2=Wiles |first2=Andrew |title=Class Fields of Abelian Extension of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> |journal=Inv. Math. |volume=76 |issue=2 |year=1984 |pages=179–330 |doi= 10.1007/bf01388599|bibcode=1984InMat..76..179M |s2cid=122576427 }}</ref> a corollary of which is a strengthening of the Herbrand–Ribet theorem: the power of ''p'' dividing ''B''<sub>''p''&minus;''n''</sub> is exactly the power of ''p'' dividing the order of ''G''<sub>''n''</sub>.
